title: Watermarking Diffusion Language Models
claim: Prior watermarks need already-generated context to compute hashes, which fails with arbitrary-order generation; ours perturbs logits in expectation and leaves detection unchanged.
layout: 3 panels separated by dashed vertical lines, left-to-right: prior works (top autoregressive, bottom diffusion), our watermark, and detector; funnel/trapezoid modules with bar-chart distributions
description: Three columns divided by dashed vertical lines. The left column, 'Prior works', stacks two token-strip examples. In the autoregressive example, the strip reads 'Wa ter mark ?'. The hash and the LLM feed a red/green split on a bar chart. In the diffusion example, the strip has masked '?' tokens on both sides of the target, so the hash is a black '?' and the caption reads 'Impossible to compute Red/Green split!'. The middle column, 'Our watermark', shows the diffusion token strip, an LLM trapezoid, and the question 'How to perturb the logits of ?'. Two teal funnels, 'Make ? green' and 'Make great green', push bar charts toward a combined watermarked distribution. The right column, 'Detector is unchanged', shows the token strip, a green/red token bar, a binomial test, and 'p = 1.3e-5 Watermarked!'. Blue, teal and green colors carry the eye through each column.
caption: An overview of why current watermarks for ARLMs fall short in the diffusion setting (left), how our watermark operates in this setting (middle) and how our watermark detector works (right).
abstract: We introduce the first watermark tailored for diffusion language models (DLMs), an emergent LLM paradigm able to generate tokens in arbitrary order, in contrast to standard autoregressive language models (ARLMs) which generate tokens sequentially. While there has been much work in ARLM watermarking, a key challenge when attempting to apply these schemes directly to the DLM setting is that they rely on previously generated tokens, which are not always available with DLM generation. In this work we address this challenge by: (i) applying the watermark in expectation over the context even when some context tokens are yet to be determined, and (ii) promoting tokens which increase the watermark strength when used as context for other tokens. This is accomplished while keeping the watermark detector unchanged. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that the DLM watermark leads to a >99% true positive rate with minimal quality impact and achieves similar robustness to existing ARLM watermarks, enabling for the first time reliable DLM watermarking.
